description: Small shaped clay counters such as cones, spheres and discs appear at Near Eastern farming sites from roughly the ninth or eighth millennium BCE. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued that each shape stood for a fixed quantity of a particular commodity, letting people keep accounts beyond memory. Her further thesis, that tokens led directly to writing, is influential but debated.
uncertainty: The function of many early tokens (counters, gaming pieces, amulets) and the direct token-to-writing sequence are contested; dates are broad ranges across many sites.

description: A stamp seal is a carved object pressed into soft clay to leave a recognisable mark. description: Before coins, silver served as money by weight. Mesopotamian texts state prices and debts in shekels, a weight unit of about 8.4 grams. The silver itself was refined from lead-bearing ores by cupellation, attested from the fourth millennium BCE.
